title: The Sheep Who Counted Children
blurb: A sheep gets the job backwards — and it works.

lesson.ask: Tilly tried one way, then another way. What is something you tried twice today?
lesson.fact: Real sheep really do sleep about four hours a night — but they nap a lot, all day long.

body: It was nearly bedtime in the green field at the top of the hill. The sun had gone soft and orange. The birds had stopped shouting and started whispering.
In the middle of that field stood one small sheep. Her name was Tilly. Tilly had one job, and everyone knew what it was.

"Count the children," said the old sheep. "That is what we do. A child lies in bed. You count. One child. Two children. Three children. And by the time you reach the sleepy ones, the child in the bed is fast asleep."
Tilly nodded. "Count the children. I can do that."
That night, Tilly stood by the fence and got ready. She took a deep breath. She looked at the sleeping houses. And then she counted.
"One CHILD," said Tilly, very loudly.
Nothing happened.
"Two CHILDREN," said Tilly, even more loudly.
Nothing happened. In a house at the bottom of the hill, a little girl sat up in bed and said, "Mum? I think there is a sheep shouting."
Tilly tried again. "THREE CHILDREN! FOUR CHILDREN! FIVE CHILDREN!"
Windows went on. Doors opened. A man in his pyjamas came outside and said, "Is everybody all right? Who is shouting numbers?"
"Me," said Tilly. "I am counting the children. It is my job. It is meant to make them sleepy."
The man in pyjamas looked at Tilly for a long moment. Then he said, "Have you tried counting something quieter?"
Tilly thought about this. She looked at the field. She looked at the sky. And then she saw them — small, soft, and moving very slowly across the dark: clouds.
"One cloud," said Tilly, quietly. "Two clouds. Three clouds."
In the house at the bottom of the hill, the little girl lay back down. The shouting had stopped. There was just a soft voice outside, going slowly past three, past four, past five.
"Six clouds," said Tilly. "Seven. Eight."
The little girl's eyes got heavy. "Nine clouds," said Tilly, and yawned. "Ten."
By eleven she had forgotten what she was counting. By twelve she was asleep with her chin on the fence, and the whole hill was quiet.
The old sheep found her there in the morning. "Did you count the children?" she asked.
"No," said Tilly. "I counted clouds. But everyone went to sleep anyway."
The old sheep thought about it for a while. Then she nodded. "Well," she said. "That is the same thing, only nicer."

And after that, every night, in that field, you could hear a small sheep going quietly through the sky: one cloud, two clouds, three — until the whole hill, sheep and children both, fell asleep together.
THE END.

title: Marvin and the Very Serious Puddle
blurb: A puddle has a very important job. Marvin has boots.

lesson.ask: The puddle was holding the sky. What is something that looks small but is actually doing a big job?
lesson.fact: A puddle holds the whole sky, upside down — every puddle is a mirror lying flat on the ground.

body: After the rain, the whole pavement was covered in puddles. Small ones. Medium ones. And one enormous one, right outside Marvin's gate, shaped like Australia.
Marvin put on his boots. Marvin's boots were yellow, and they made a sound that Marvin liked very much: squelch.
"Marvin," said his mother. "If you jump in that puddle, you will be wet from your hat to your socks."
Marvin looked at the puddle. The puddle looked back, very calmly, the way a puddle does.
"I understand," said Marvin.
He was not lying. He understood completely. He understood that the puddle was enormous, that his boots were yellow, and that some things in life are simply meant to be jumped in.
So he jumped.
SPLASH.
It was a magnificent splash. It went up. It went sideways. It went into the hedge, where a blackbird was sitting, minding its own business. The blackbird made a noise like a rusty door and flew away.
Marvin stood in the middle of the puddle, wet from his hat to his socks, feeling extremely good.
And then the puddle spoke.
"Excuse me," said the puddle.
Marvin froze.
"I said excuse me," said the puddle. "I am working."
"Working?" said Marvin.

"Working," said the puddle. "I am an enormous puddle. Do you know how much sky I have to hold? I am holding the entire sky, upside down, all day. Clouds. Birds. One aeroplane, twice. It is a very big job and I am doing it very well, and then somebody in yellow boots comes along and jumps straight through the middle of my sky."
Marvin looked down. He could see the sky in the puddle, in pieces now, wobbling.
"I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't know you were busy."
"Nobody ever does," said the puddle, rather sadly. "Puddles look like nothing. That is exactly why we get jumped on."
Marvin stood still in the water and thought about being looked at and thought to be nothing. He did not like the way it felt.
"Can I help?" he said.
The puddle went quiet for a moment. "Well," it said. "You could stop standing in the middle of me."
Marvin stepped out, carefully, and stood on the dry bit by the gate.
Slowly, very slowly, the puddle got its sky back. A cloud came in. Then a whole tree, upside down. Then the sun, which was pleased to be included.
"Better," said the puddle. "Much better. Thank you."
And Marvin found that he was wet, and cold, and had a hole in one sock, and he did not mind one bit. He had made friends with a puddle, which is not a thing most people manage before breakfast.

The next morning, the puddle had gone somewhere to do its next job. But it had left something behind: a perfectly round, flat, dry circle of pavement, exactly the size of a puddle, and right in the middle of it, one small feather — the blackbird's, from the day before.
Marvin kept it in a tin.
And he never jumped in an enormous puddle again, unless he had first asked politely.
THE END.

title: The Loudest Sock in the World
blurb: A new sock arrives. The sock has opinions.

lesson.ask: The sock could not be quiet. How did {{name}} help it?
lesson.fact: Your feet have about a quarter of all the bones in your body — 52 of them, and your toes do half the work of balancing.

body: On Monday, {{namePos}} opened the drawer and found a new sock. It was red, with one green stripe, and the moment the drawer opened, the sock said:
"HELLO!"
{{name}} jumped.
"I AM THE LOUDEST SOCK IN THE WORLD," said the sock, happily. "AND I HAVE BEEN IN THIS DRAWER FOR SIX DAYS."
"Socks can't talk," said {{name}}.
"WRONG," said the sock. "Socks can't talk QUIETLY. That is different, and it is my whole problem."
So {{name}} put the sock on. It was warm. It was comfortable. It also shouted comments about everything it saw.
"WHAT A BIG KITCHEN," said the sock. "IS THAT THE KETTLE? I LIKE IT. I LIKE EVERYTHING HERE."
At breakfast, {{name}} put the sock's foot under the table. "Please," whispered {{name}}. "Please be quieter. People are looking."
"OKAY," said the sock. Then, a second later: "THE TOAST IS VERY GOOD."

At school, things got worse. During quiet reading, the sock said, "I CANNOT SEE THE PICTURES FROM DOWN HERE." During maths, the sock said, "NINE LOOKS LIKE A BALLOON." During the bit where everyone had to be completely silent, the sock said, in its biggest voice: "THIS IS MY FAVOURITE PART!"
Twenty-three children turned to look at {{name}}'s foot.
After school, {{name}} sat on the front step and had a serious talk with the sock.
"You are getting me in trouble," said {{name}}. "You have to learn to be quiet, or you have to live in the drawer."
The sock was quiet for a long time. So long that {{name}} thought it had gone. Then it said, in a small voice:
"I don't know how."
{{name}} thought about this. It is hard to know how to do something nobody has shown you.
"Right," said {{name}}. "We'll practise. When I press your toe, that means quiet. When I squeeze your heel, that means you can talk."
"And nothing else?" said the sock.
"Nothing else," said {{name}}.
They practised all evening. Press the toe — quiet. Squeeze the heel — "HELLO." Press the toe — quiet.
By bedtime, the sock could do it.
That night {{name}} wore the sock to bed, which was unusual, but the sock was warm and had had a hard week.
"Squeeze or press?" whispered the sock.
"Squeeze," said {{name}}.
The sock thought for a moment. Then it said, as quietly as it could — which for the loudest sock in the world was still not very quiet, but it was trying:
"Goodnight. I like you. I like everything here."
And {{name}} fell asleep, warm, with one green stripe showing above the covers.
THE END.

title: Barnaby and the Slowest Race
blurb: Barnaby is built for speed. The lettuce can wait.

lesson.ask: Barnaby was very proud of his speed. What is something you took your time doing today?
lesson.fact: A garden snail's top speed is about one metre an hour, and they can sleep for days at a time.

body: In the vegetable patch behind the kitchen, Barnaby the snail was polishing his shell with a drop of morning dew.
Barnaby was not an ordinary snail. Barnaby was built for pure racing.
"Look at these curves," Barnaby said to a nearby worm. "Aerodynamic. Crisp. Unstoppable."
The worm poked its head out of the soil, blinked once, and went back down.
"Jealousy," said Barnaby, nodding wisely. "A common reaction to greatness."
That afternoon, {{name}} sat on the warm stone step, tying up a red sneaker.
Barnaby slid onto the gravel path and drew a line in the dust with his tail.
"You. In the red shoes," announced Barnaby. "Race me to the flowerpot. If you dare."
{{name}} looked down at the tiny brown spiral on the path.
"The big flowerpot?" said {{name}}. "That is six steps away."
"Six steps for an amateur," Barnaby scoffed. "A grand tour for a professional. Three, two, one—GO!"
{{name}} took six steps and reached the flowerpot in four seconds.
Then {{name}} turned around and sat down to watch.
Barnaby was already moving. He was giving it everything he had.
A leaf blew past him. Then an ant carrying half a potato chip overtook him on the inside lane.
"Drafting," Barnaby muttered between his teeth. "Very clever ant. But he cannot hold that pace."
By tea-time, Barnaby had passed the first pebble.
By bath-time, Barnaby was halfway past a dry twig, leaving a sparkling silver ribbon behind him.
"Look at that acceleration," Barnaby whispered to a sleeping beetle. "I am practically flying."
When {{name}} came outside in pyjamas to say goodnight, the garden had turned purple and blue.
Barnaby had finally arrived at the edge of the pot.
"A photo finish," wheezed Barnaby happily. "I think I took it by a whisker."
{{name}} gently placed a fresh, cool lettuce leaf right next to him.
Barnaby took one tiny bite, yawned a snail-sized yawn, and pulled his head into his shell.
"Engine cooling down," came a muffled voice from inside the shell. "Rematch tomorrow. After breakfast."
And the garden went quiet, under the silver path of the moon.
THE END.

title: The Teapot That Wanted to Sing
blurb: A blue teapot tries to sing opera. The cups prefer a lullaby.

lesson.ask: The teapot learned that quiet songs are very special. What is your favourite quiet sound?
lesson.fact: The steam that comes out of a kettle is water turning from liquid into gas, which expands by over a thousand times.

body: On the middle shelf in the kitchen lived a round blue teapot named Arthur.
Arthur had a spout shaped like a trumpet and a handle like a fancy ear.
"Kettles only whistle," Arthur liked to say. "Whistling is vulgar. I, on the other hand, was built for opera."
The two white teacups beside him groaned.
"Please not the opera," said the big cup. "It is only Tuesday."
That evening, {{namePos}} grandfather filled Arthur with boiling water and three peppermint leaves.
As the water warmed his ceramic belly, Arthur felt the music rising.
"ME-ME-ME-MEEEE!" Arthur announced through his spout.
A high, wobbly blast of steam shot out and hit the toaster.
"Arthur," said the toaster, without looking up. "You are flat. And you are getting crumbs damp."
"That was just my warm-up," Arthur replied with great dignity.
He took another deep breath of steam. "LA-LA-LAAAAAA!"
The spoons in the drawer began to jingle. The salt shaker hopped half an inch to the left.
{{name}} walked into the kitchen in bunny slippers, rubbing one eye.
"Who is making that funny squeak?" asked {{name}}.
Arthur stopped. "A squeak? I am delivering a dramatic masterpiece."
"It sounds like a mouse blowing a party horn," said {{name}}, smiling.
Arthur considered this. He looked at his reflection in the shiny kettle.
"A party horn?" he muttered, rather wounded.
"Bedtime needs quiet music," {{name}} whispered, gently touching Arthur's warm handle. "Soft, like the rain."
Arthur let out a long, slow breath.
The steam didn't blast this time. It curled up in a lazy, quiet spiral towards the ceiling.
"Huuuummmmm," went Arthur, very gently. "Huuuum-shhhhh."
It sounded like the wind outside a cozy window, or a purring cat wrapped in a blanket.
The teacups settled happily into their saucers.
"Much better," murmured {{name}}, taking the peppermint tea.
The kitchen lights clicked off, leaving Arthur on the shelf, humming the sleepiest note he knew until the whole house was fast asleep.
THE END.

title: The Button Who Steered the Coat
blurb: A top button is convinced it drives the whole winter coat.

lesson.ask: Pip was very proud of his driving. What was your favourite adventure today?
lesson.fact: Buttons with holes were used for decoration for thousands of years before anyone thought to invent a buttonhole.

body: Pip was a bright red button sewn to the very top of {{namePos}} winter coat.
He had four neat holes and four tight threads of yellow cotton.
Pip was extremely important, and he never let the other buttons forget it.
"The zipper is just the engine," Pip explained every morning. "The sleeves are the wings. But I—I am the steering wheel."
Down below, the middle button gave a tiny wobble. "I thought the child did the walking."
"Nonsense," said Pip. "Watch this."
{{name}} put the coat on, zipped it up, and popped Pip securely into his buttonhole.
Click.
"Engine engaged," whispered Pip. "Prepare for departure."
Out the front door they went, into the crisp autumn wind.
When {{name}} turned left toward the playground, Pip puffed out his chest.
"Hard left!" Pip shouted into the breeze. "Magnificent turn! Perfect navigation!"
They went past the bakery. The smell of warm cinnamon filled the air.
"Bypassing the bakery," Pip noted formally. "Staying on course. You may thank me later, stomach."
At the park, {{name}} ran around the big oak tree three times.
"Slalom course!" Pip cried, thrilled. "Hold on to your threads! We are cornering at high speeds!"
The bottom button was hanging on for dear life. "Can we please go straight? I feel dizzy."
"No time for weakness!" said Pip. "Destination ahead: the slide!"
All afternoon, Pip steered past bicycles, around prams, and safely through the front gate.
When dusk settled over the street, the streetlamps flickered orange.
Inside the warm hallway, {{name}} unbuttoned Pip with a gentle tug.
"Docking sequence initiated," Pip whispered, feeling the yellow threads relax.
The coat was hung smoothly on its wooden peg behind the front door.
Pip looked down the row of buttons in the quiet, dim hall.
"Another successful journey," Pip murmured, his shiny red face catching the nightlight.
"Good driving, Captain," whispered the middle button.
Pip smiled, tucked his threads in against the wool, and shut his four eyes for the night.
THE END.

title: George and the Tiny Warm Puff
blurb: A fierce dragon tries to roar fire. Out comes warm buttered toast.

lesson.ask: George was sad he could not breathe fire, but his toast puff was even better. What makes you feel cozy?
lesson.fact: Many lizards and reptiles like to bask on warm rocks because they rely on outside warmth to stay cozy.

body: George was a dragon, and he wanted everyone to remember it.
He had emerald green scales, two pointy wings the size of maple leaves, and a tail that ended in a sharp little triangle.
There was only one problem: George was the size of a teacup, and he had a secret he considered deeply humiliating.
In the evenings, George would sit on the hearth rug, plant his tiny claws, and practice his ferocious roar.
"BEHOLD THE TERROR OF THE MOUNTAIN!" George shouted.
He sucked in a huge breath of air. His scales rippled. His eyes narrowed.
POOF.
A small, pale cloud of smoke floated out of his nostrils.
It didn't smell like burning logs or scorched stone. It smelled exactly, undeniably, like hot buttered toast.
"Unacceptable," grumbled George, fanning the cloud away with his tail. "Simply embarrassing."
{{name}} sat down on the rug cross-legged, holding a bedtime storybook.
"I think it smells lovely," {{name}} said.
"I am a beast of ancient legend," George said stiffly. "I am not a breakfast appliance."
"Try again," encouraged {{name}}. "Maybe aim for the chimney."
George puffed his chest until he looked like a round green tennis ball.
"FLEE BEFORE MY WRATH!" George cried.
Puff.
Another warm little cloud drifted out, this time smelling faintly of cinnamon.
George slumped onto his belly and buried his snout in his paws.
"Ruined," he sighed. "A dragon who belongs in a bakery."
The room was getting chilly as the night wind tapped at the windowpane.
{{name}} pulled the thick woolen blanket down over cold feet and gave a little shiver.
George peeked out from behind his paws. "Are your toes freezing?"
"A bit," {{name}} admitted.
George crept over, curled himself into a neat green doughnut right across {{namePos}} slippers, and let out three slow, gentle puffs.
The blanket grew delightfully warm, cozy and soft.
"See?" whispered {{name}}, pulling the covers up to the chin. "Fierce dragons could never do that."
George rested his chin on his tail, purred a sleepy rumble that smelled of warm bread, and closed his eyes.
THE END.

title: The Moonbeam Who Wanted a Nap
blurb: A tired moonbeam tries to find somewhere dark enough to sleep.

lesson.ask: Orlo searched for a quiet, cozy spot to rest. What is your favourite thing about bedtime?
lesson.fact: Moonlight is actually sunlight bouncing off the rocky surface of the moon like a giant mirror.

body: High up in the night sky, while the stars were getting ready for work, a small silver moonbeam named Orlo was already yawning.
"I don't see why the sun gets the day shift," Orlo complained to the moon.
"The sun is very reliable," said the moon.
"The sun gets picnics and beach towels," said Orlo. "I get owls and empty car parks. And I am exhausted."
"You have responsibilities," the moon told him gently. "Go down there and shine on something noble."
Orlo slid down to Earth on a long, cool beam of light.
But Orlo had no intention of shining on anything noble. Orlo wanted a nap.
He tried sliding into the garden shed through the keyhole.
But the moment Orlo entered the shed, the watering can lit up like a disco ball, and three rakes cast long, dramatic shadows.
"Too bright," groaned Orlo. "I am ruining my own darkness."
Next, he tried sneaking under a large flat rock near the pond.
A toad looked at him in dismay. "Excuse me," said the toad. "I was sleeping. You are like a flashlight in my bedroom."
"Sorry," Orlo sighed, backing out.
Finally, Orlo drifted through an open window upstairs, right into {{namePos}} bedroom.
The room was quiet. A tiny nightlight hummed in the corner.
{{name}} was lying in bed, blinking sleepily at the ceiling.
"Who is that on the rug?" {{name}} whispered.
"It's me," said Orlo, curling in a silver ring by the wardrobe. "I am a moonbeam on strike. I need somewhere dark, but everywhere I go, I shine."
{{name}} thought about this for a moment.
"Come over here," said {{name}}.
Orlo crept across the wooden floorboards, climbing up the side of the bed until he rested on the blue quilt.
{{name}} gently lifted the edge of the blanket and tucked Orlo right underneath, folding the dark wool over the silver light.
Under the quilt, the glow went soft and milky, like a warm glass of milk in the dark.
"Is that better?" whispered {{name}}.
"It is perfection," breathed Orlo from beneath the blanket.
He dimmed his light down to a faint, gentle shimmer, not much brighter than a firefly.
In the quiet room, {{name}} closed heavy eyes, while outside, the great silver moon smiled down upon the sleeping house.
THE END.
